parsed_answer.content: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) is the fourth of the SOLID principles, formulated by Robert C. Martin. It states that a software client should never be forced to implement an interface that it does not use, or alternatively, that users should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. In real-world enterprise architectures—especially when designing complex Input/Output (I/O) systems, NIO channels, and exception handling hierarchies—violating ISP leads to bloated contracts, tightly coupled code, and unnecessary stubbing of methods that carry no semantic meaning for a given implementation. Instead of creating massive, monolithic interfaces that attempt to cater to every possible requirement, ISP demands the granular breakup of contracts into cohesive, client-specific roles.

In the context of Java I/O and NIO (New I/O), we can observe ISP in action within the java.nio.channels package. Rather than having a single mega-channel interface that handles reading, writing, connecting, accepting, and multiplexing, the designers split these operations into segregated interfaces like ReadableByteChannel, WritableByteChannel, GatheringByteChannel, and ScatteringByteChannel. This segregation allows a file channel or a socket channel to implement precisely the capabilities it supports without throwing UnsupportedOperationException for irrelevant operations. Similarly, robust exception handling strategies benefit from ISP by segregating custom exception-reporting interfaces, ensuring that exception handlers only bind to the specific failure domains they are equipped to remediate.

rows: Clients depend on methods they never call, creating fragile recompilation cascades.
Clients depend solely on the precise methods matching their domain logic.
Encourages throwing UnsupportedOperationException for unimplemented contract methods.
Eliminates unsupported operation patterns entirely through strict type constraints.
Unit tests require massive, cumbersome mock setups with numerous dummy method returns.
Tests are lightweight, targeting singular, highly focused mock behaviors.

items: ISP shifts design focus from 'what an object is' to 'what a client needs to interact with', mapping closely to role-based interface design.
In high-performance NIO architectures, segregating channel capabilities allows selectors and buffers to operate against narrow type bounds, maximizing polymorphism safety.
Refactoring a fat interface into segregated ones often reveals hidden abstractions and improves the overall cohesion of domain services.

parsed_answer.content: A common trap when applying ISP is over-segregating to the point of interface explosion—creating an interface for every single method. Strike a balance by grouping methods by client role. If two distinct clients always use the same subset of methods together, keep them in a single segregated interface.
